name: Popcorn
lede: Popcorn is a warm, pale gold named for the snack, and the color books say almost nothing about it as a color.

sections.title: A name the books do not use
sections.body: Searching our twenty-nine color books turns up the word *popcorn* only twice as a plain word, and in neither case does it name a color [1][2]. Birren uses popcorn as an example of a food that tastes of less on a roller coaster, in a passage on senses influencing each other [1]. St Clair uses it for a shape: in 1925 Joan Miró left a large canvas almost blank, with a popcorn-shaped daub of forget-me-not blue-colored paint [2]. So the name here is a modern descriptive one, a shade a little deeper than [[cream]] and warmer than [[beige]], and its origin as a color name is undocumented.

sections.title: Field notes
sections.body: In our archive of 23,781 paintings, a color within six units of this swatch covers at least five per cent of the canvas in 826 works, about 3.5 per cent [3]. It is common in Asian paper-and-silk painting: 37 of the 96 Kalighat works and 73 of the 721 Indian works carry it [3]. The oldest strong cases include Kanô Tsunenobu's album of fan-shaped paintings of 1636 and Suzuki Kiitsu's flower paintings of 1801 [3]. As always these are photographs of aged paintings, so read them as screen colors [3].

questions.q: In which kind of painting is this golden color common in our archive?
True or false: the color books treat popcorn as an established color name.

openers: The color books never use popcorn as a color: Miró's popcorn-shaped daub is the closest they come.
